draft.title: Very large and very small units
card: A prefix is a word placed before a unit to show a power of 10. It saves writing many zeros.
Large
kilo is \(10^{3}\), mega is \(10^{6}\), giga is \(10^{9}\), tera is \(10^{12}\). So 1 gigabyte is \(10^{9}\) bytes.
Small
milli is \(10^{-3}\), micro is \(10^{-6}\), nano is \(10^{-9}\). So 1 nanometre is \(10^{-9}\) metres.
To change units, replace the prefix with its power of 10. Example: 5 megawatts is \(5 \times 10^{6}\) watts, which is 5{,}000{,}000 watts.
draft.remember: Each prefix stands for a power of 10: positive powers for large units, negative powers for small ones.

a.q: Which power of 10 does the prefix giga stand for?
a.why: Giga means \(10^{9}\), or one billion. Mega is only \(10^{6}\), and nano is the small unit \(10^{-9}\), which has the same size of power but a negative sign.
a.clue: Giga is a large prefix, and it sits between mega and tera.

b.q: A virus particle in a Sydney lab is 100 nanometres wide. How wide is it in metres?
b.why: Nano is \(10^{-9}\), so the width is \(100 \times 10^{-9}\), which is \(10^{2} \times 10^{-9} = 10^{-7}\) m. Using \(10^{-6}\) would be the micro prefix, which is a different unit.
b.clue: Write 100 as a power of 10, then combine it with the nano power.

problems.detail: "5{,}000{,}000 watts" is outside the \( \) delimiters, so the LaTeX braces will show as literal text (5{,}000{,}000). It should be written as \(5\,000\,000\) inside LaTeX, or as plain 5 000 000.
